## The Museum of Almost

Every morning, before the doors opened, Lina unlocked three hundred and twelve rooms.

The museum occupied a narrow building between a dry cleaner and a bank that never seemed to have customers. From the street, it looked ordinary. Inside, the rooms continued farther than the building should have allowed.

Their exhibits were lives.

Not whole lives, exactly. More often, they were single moments: the conversation you abandoned halfway through, the train you missed, the question you answered when another answer might have changed everything.

Lina’s favorite exhibit was a brass key.

> **THE APARTMENT ON CANAL STREET**  
> You moved in on a wet Tuesday. The balcony faced south. You never learned what the view looked like because you were always looking for the key.

She had always found the museum slightly cruel. People entered curious and left convinced that their real lives were the wrong version.

One rainy afternoon, a boy came through the ticket booth with his sleeves buttoned incorrectly and a red scarf streaming behind him.

“What’s the most famous person’s almost-life?” he asked.

Lina considered this. “Why do you want to see that?”

“To see if they were happy.”

“Almost-lives aren’t allowed to be completely different. Otherwise they’re just imaginary lives. In this museum, everything is the same except one thing.”

He frowned. “So they can be better?”

“Sometimes. But we don’t display those.”

He looked personally offended. “Why not?”

“Because people would spend all day touring rooms where they were braver, kinder, more successful. Then they’d go home and treat their actual lives as failures.”

The boy considered this with the solemnity available only to children and philosophers.

“My mother says I should be less shy,” he said.

“Was there a room where you spoke?”

“Yes.”

“Did you like what happened?”

“No. Everyone laughed.”

Lina crouched to his level. “That sounds like a terrible almost-life.”

He nodded. “I’d rather go back to the one where I don’t speak.”

So she gave him a paper ticket stamped ADMITTED ANYWAY and sent him into the Hall of Ordinary Tuesdays, where he spent twenty minutes examining a life in which he had forgotten his lines at the school play.

That was how Lina understood she had been wrong about the museum.

For years, she had assumed its purpose was to preserve regret. But regret was only one kind of weather passing through a room. The exhibits also held the conversations that might have comforted you, the chances that might have rescued you, the small mercies you would never know you needed.

One exhibit was an unsent letter.

Another was the five minutes after a mistake, before anyone had told you it wouldn’t matter.

Another was a telephone ringing in an empty kitchen.

You could put your ear to the receiver. Each time, a different person answered.

“Mum?”

“Hello?”

“I’m sorry about the other thing.”

Their voices never revealed what had happened before or after. You listened until the connection faded, carrying away a feeling that was almost relief.

At closing, Lina counted the unlocked rooms. Three hundred and twelve.

Three hundred and thirteen doors waited in the last corridor.

This one had no plaque.

Lina fetched the master key and tried it in the lock. It turned easily.

Inside was a bare room with tall windows, a workbench, and stacks of blueprints. Hammers hung from hooks. Paint cans waited beside an unfinished wall. Beyond the glass, a city moved through evening light, unaware that everything could still be built.

On the workbench lay a list of measurements and a note in Lina’s handwriting.

*Not what you imagined. Not what you missed. What you’re making now.*

She heard footsteps in the corridor.

The founder of the museum appeared there, carrying his coat and an armful of forgotten brochures. He was an old man with careful eyes and an unfortunate talent for noticing everything.

“A new exhibit?” he asked.

“I suppose so.”

“Interesting.”

He glanced at the blueprints, then at Lina, and smiled as if he already knew what she thought.

“Don’t rush it,” he said. “Most doors don’t open all at once.”

Later, after the last visitors had gone and the lights had been dimmed, Lina stood alone before the new room.

For once, she did not want to unlock anything.

She wanted to return in the morning, measure the windows, choose the colors, and begin.

The room before the room, the founder had called it.

But Lina had always preferred the simpler name.

*The beginning.*
